Okay, thanks so much, Bernardia, for highlighting the importance of enabling environments and for also being a sort of change agent when it comes to equipping mayors with the knowledge of how to construct those enabling environments for synergies. Over to you, Scott.

Thank you everyone for having me today. Appreciate it. All my colleagues here. Thank you, Minister. There is a trade-off with companies. You're always making a trade-off in this world no matter what, right? And I think when you think about it, you start with the C-suite, right? Any C-suite at any big company, they have to drive a mission, they have to drive values. I'll start with the mission of our company and I'll relay that to everything else. The mission of our company is to create a positive human impact in the world. We hear a lot of E and G in the room today. We're kind of right in the middle with the S, right? So, when I'm talking to C-suites, when I'm talking to executives, we're talking about the social aspects of these businesses, right? And there is a compromise there. So, when I look in this, And I've seen it across the board from just about every Fortune 500 CEO. And it's a challenge to us because they always— when we find forced labor, we find slave labor, what's the first thing they do? They want to shut down the company. We can't do that. The average working age in certain countries is 13 years old. If you don't have a job by then, you potentially are sold into slavery or you're trafficked, right? So what is the compromise? If they don't see it, they don't know about it, they don't have to action it. So bringing what I do to light is a very large challenge. And to drive synergies in what I do to the executives, I have to make it relatable. I have to— and I hate to use this, but I have children and a lot of people in this room have children. Leave the world a better place for your kids than you came into it is my driving principle. And if I can relate to their children, I can relate to the broader audience. And everybody has kids in those boardrooms. And when you do that, you can drive synergies for them to move in the right direction. So you have to find something relatable with the audience you're dealing with to really kind of turn the screws into them to make a good decision. And that's what I do.

Thanks so much, Scott, for highlighting the importance of trying to make some of these arguments most relatable and also making human connections there. I think this is a really important point. We have a representative from the Children and Youth Major Group to UNEP. Thank you so much, Eric. Distinguished speakers, guests, colleagues, good morning, good afternoon. My name is Fitriyah. I'm Indonesian, Izimbu, Bermudan, Bernadia. I'm currently pursuing a master's degree in public health and environmental health sciences at Rutgers University and serving as the environmental health focal point for Children and Youth Major Group at UNEP. So, as a schooler and then now aspire to be a researcher, I truly understand how this is really important for us to work in CYMG, especially for now, to make our advocacy based on the evidence-based data. So, I want to depart this answer from the current resolution that has been adopted last year in the UNEP 7, Resolution 7/6, enhancing meaningful participation of young people in the environmental process and education. I think that's our big milestone that we are glad to share here because we've been working really hard to have this resolution finally passed and then supported by the member states. Now, we, as the formal engagement for young people within the UNEP, we have this more mandate to facilitate young people to engage within this space. ACYMG itself, Within these past 2 years, we have emerged supporting the establishment of 3 networks. The first one, the Ocean Science and Governance Youth Network. Second one, recently launched, Youth Plastic Action Network. And then the last one is Young Science Policy Network, or YSPN. We realize that this is really important for us to also support the science policy interface and then help facilitate young people who are having this interest, especially in the YSPN, the Young Science Policy Network, to, you know, I think the minister mentioned how it's fragmented, you know, how young people participation, young scientists also fragmented. And then here we're trying to build synergy between young people who are having background in the diverse knowledge and then diverse experience. And within our YSPN, we have 3 core issues that we want to work on more. The first one on the climate action. Second is nature, biodiversity, land, and ecosystem. And then the last one, quite happening, is chemical waste and pollutions. So through this platform, we are trying to build this collaborations between the young people to engage in the various multilateral environmental agreements, science policy interfaces, so we can provide better advocacy avenues for young people, not only on the advocacy section, but also in the research section. So I think that's how, you know, we are trying to express our engagement and our spirit to engage with this decision-making process and then research process, while also it's really important to us to be able to get these recognitions, this support to sit at the same table with the equal voices, and then also considering our expertise to also as equal as the other expertise for you know, for this human and then planetary health. I think that's all my questions— my answers, sorry. Thank you, Eric.

Okay, thank you so much, Fitriyah, for also reminding us that some of the other UNEA resolutions focused on youth empowerment, and also for highlighting, I think, one of the key points of synergies that we sometimes miss when we talk about multiple environmental benefits is that these interactions are also critical between, you know, different people. So when you bring together different youth, you can also deliver a stronger case for collective action and help solve some of these environmental issues. Really important perspective there. And I think that also loops us back around to a little bit more about how governments and also international processes can play a role in promoting synergies. And so I'd like to basically conclude the multi-stakeholder dialogue with a question to the Deputy Foreign Minister from Armenia. This is Robert Agbegsogmanian. And so, Deputy Foreign Minister, looking ahead to the CBD COP17 that's going to be hosted in Armenia and beyond, How can international processes help strengthen synergies across climate, biodiversity, pollution control, and sustainable development more generally?

Thank you very much, Excellencies, distinguished colleagues, ladies and gentlemen. First of all, I would like to express my appreciation to co-organizers for convening this important discussion and for the opportunity to participate and share some thoughts as incoming presidency of the As presidency of COP17, we are committed to advancing practical, inclusive, and action-oriented cooperation across the Rio Conventions, and I see that there is a consensus in this room that climate change, biodiversity laws, and pollution are interconnected challenges that cannot be addressed in isolation, and fragmented approaches that do not take into account cross-cutting issues cannot yield effective results. And during these 2 years when Armenia was elected as incoming president of COP17, on some instances we have faced very worrisome phenomena when decisions adopted during one COP can contradict or even worse can affect the decisions adopted during the other COPs. And I believe we should work together, join up our our efforts in order to address this issue. And in this regard, I believe the joint statement on synergies, co-signed by current and incoming presidencies of Rio conventions during last year during COP13, Belém demonstrated growing political momentum for synergies and cooperation on the implementation. So the CBD COP17 can build on this political momentum and reinforce the support of the international community for synergies. Actually, on the other hand, I also believe that the triple planetary crisis cannot be addressed by governments alone, and here for effective implementation we need the whole-of-government and whole-of-society approach, bringing together governments, indigenous peoples and local communities, civil society, youth, academia, philanthropy, private sector, etc. So the synergies are best implemented at the national level through the integrated planning and coordinated implementation. Armenia's own experience demonstrates this. We have aligned our updated NBSAP with our NDC, helping strengthen institutional coordination, reduce duplication, and focus national efforts on implementation. And it comes actually to COP17, as you As you may know, as a central element of the COP17 process, the global review of the collective progress in implementation of the KMGBF will serve as a key mechanism for assessing collective progress towards the goals and targets of the framework, identifying the gaps, and informing the next steps of implementation. It presents a landmark opportunity to strengthen the science science policy interface by drawing on scientific assessment together with national experience and traditional knowledge. Looking ahead, countries should enhance coherence among national planning, monitoring, and review mechanisms, ensuring that these processes reinforce one another. And as incoming presidency of CBD COP17, we and ready to work with all the parties and stakeholders to strengthen synergy across sectors in support of sustainable, sustainable future. And using this opportunity, I would like to invite all of you to make part of the COP17 in Yerevan in October this year. Thank you very much.
Thank you very much.

Okay, thank you very much, Deputy Foreign Minister, for also reminding us that there's been some recent discussions on trying to use synergies to strengthen coordination across these different agreements, and also highlighting some of the good work that Armenia is doing, for instance, by integrating NDCs and NBSAPs, and also for inviting us to come and experience what I think will be momentous progress at the, at the CBD COP in Armenia coming up. So now what I'd like to do is, um, just to frame how, how we've moved things along. You know, we've, we've heard a little bit about, um, the importance of synergies, um, from many different perspectives, whether it be focusing sort of on the ground, focusing on local governments and cities, and using different platforms for scaling up synergies We've heard a little bit about how to make synergies relatable, especially from a business perspective, and bringing in some of the human dimension as well, and recognize the importance of youth and young people as ways to bridge the science-policy-practice interface, and also to bring together different young people to motivate collective action on synergies. And last but not least, we've also heard a little bit about the importance once again of these international processes and how synergies can be mainstreamed in international processes, and hopefully that also can drive the scaling of synergies. What I'd like to do now is turn us over to a bit of interventions from the floor, and as I mentioned at the very beginning, we've identified a few colleagues prior to the event that are going to provide provide some comments and interventions based upon what we've already heard. And so first, I'd like to come over— I'm going to head over to this side of the table right now. And so I'd like to ask a colleague from the United Arab Emirates. This is Ms. Hanan Ali, the Managing Director for Federal Competitiveness and Competitiveness and Statistics Center, and she's also the chair of the UAE National Committee on SDGs. And I'd like her to reflect a little bit upon what she's heard today and raise some points that are salient from, from her perspective.

Thank you, Chair, Excellencies, distinguished colleagues. It's very inspiring and enlightening to hear the different dialogues, and I am sure dialogues like this would help us get closer to impact. And that's the most important thing. As we enter the final year of the 2030 Agenda, one lesson has become increasingly clear. The challenges before us— climate change, water scarcity, food security, biodiversity loss, and energy transition— do not exist in isolation. It requires an integrated approach. The policies designed to address them and science are critical for bridging these gaps. This is one of the key reflections of the UAE's 3rd Voluntary National Review. Our experience has shown that sustainable development accelerators when science accelerates when science helps governments understand the connection between challenges and designed integrated solutions. One example is our approach to water resilience through the UAE's. Water Security Strategy 2036, we are bringing together engineering, environmental science, clean energy, and infrastructure planning to reduce water demand, expand wastewater reuse, and transition towards lower-carbon desalination. Therefore, one policy framework is advancing SDGs 6, 7, 11, and 13 simultaneously. Science is also transforming how we govern across the UAE. Digital platforms, geospatial technologies, and artificial intelligence are strengthening the link between evidence and decision-making, enabling the government to move from periodic reporting towards more continuous adaptive policymaking. Finally, I should note that success of building these connections has been underpinned by partnerships, partnerships that brings together the relevant actors from across the sectors. As our 3rd Voluntary National Review demonstrates, the future of sustainable development will depend not only on stronger science or stronger policies, but stronger connections between them. Thank you.

Thank you so much, Ms. Ali, for highlighting the importance role— important role of science-based decision-making, especially when it comes to sustainable water management and the multiple benefits or synergies that can come from that type of approach. And also making this point about, you know, connecting or making connections between different goals. This is a really salient point, especially in the water space. Now I'd like to hear a little bit of perspective from a colleague from the Canadian UN Youth Delegate Program. This is Nathaniel Ip. Nathaniel, I'd like to hear some of your reflections.

Thank you, Eric, and thank you to the co-conveners for organizing this really important event. Excellencies, distinguished delegates, and dear colleagues, I have the privilege of speaking on behalf of the UN Youth Delegate Planetary Health Coalition. As a Canadian UN Youth Delegate working alongside counterparts from 6 continents, we examined the triple planetary crisis through a planetary health lens, building on health as a driver of ambition mentioned earlier by Eric. Our message was consistent across regions. Climate change, biodiversity loss, and pollution are undoubtedly interconnected crises driving wildfires in Canada, food insecurity in South Africa, threats to water security due to glacial retreat in Peru, and ecosystem degradation that undermines both human and planetary well-being. Delegates also emphasized the importance of Indigenous leadership, ecological stewardship, and sustainable food systems. We also identified a persistent gap between evidence and action, as others have outlined today. Our dialogue revealed that this policy-action gap drives climate anxiety in young people. To help close this gap, one of the ways we can work together is on youth citizen science and recognizing it as a valuable source of evidence. Across regions, we found that youth are already monitoring biodiversity, documenting pollution, tracking wildfire impacts, and recording environmental change within their communities. These efforts can complement traditional scientific data and meaningfully integrate youth perspectives into policy processes, which can in turn strengthen the science-policy-practice interface and ensure that responses to the planetary— triple planetary crisis are grounded in both evidence and lived experience. Thank you.

Thanks so much for highlighting this sort of action gap, Nathaniel, and underlining the point that, you know, youth can be critical to help demonstrate how you deliver action on the ground. I happen to have a 10-year-old daughter. In Japan. And living in Japan, it's really amazing to me as how well students are aware of the SDGs and how they try to practice them in their everyday life. And I think this is something that you're also pointing to. So thanks very much for bringing this out. And then I think I'd like to now turn the conversation over to our colleagues from Oxford University, or the University of Oxford, and and the Oxford Poverty and Human Development Initiative. This is Sabina Alkira, and I think they will reflect a little bit on some of the work that they're doing to try to bring some of the environmental and human development issues together. So, Sabina, over to you.

Thank you so much, Excellencies, distinguished guests, friends. Thank you for having me. I commend the authors of the report on looking at the synergies between the triple planetary crises, and the word synergy to me brings to mind bowling. In bowling, you want to have one ball but you want to drop 3 pins, 10 pins, get a strike. And so the synergistic approaches are so valuable, cost-saving, and visible. I'd like to add one more, not crisis, but one more consideration, which is poverty, which is what we work on, multidimensional poverty. We look at the different deprivations that strike the same person and household at the same time. And the definitions of poverty differ. Armenia has an official MPI, so does Panama, so do 56 countries. I'll give an example, one example from the Global Multidimensional Poverty Index we do with UNDP. It covers 6.3 billion people in the developing world. 1.1 billion are multidimensionally poor, experiencing deprivations across undernutrition, out-of-school children, water sanitation, electricity, assets, and housing. Of those 1.1 billion poor people, 887 experienced at least one climate hazard in their subnational region the same time they were poor: extreme heat, air pollution, flood, or drought. 887 million. So that's 80% of all poor people. And among those people, their poverty was higher if they experienced more at the same time. So 651 had 2 climate situations at the same time they were poor. 309 experienced 3 climate hazards at the same time. And so I think bringing into focus these impoverished communities, you see another resource. You see people who can host ecotourism, people who can build flood resistant housing, people who can think about the ways of cleansing the environment. So I think that trying to— as some of the 147 case studies did this, but bringing them in as collaborators, bringing the youth, the impoverished youth in as innovators is another way to broaden and ground this and also to integrate it with another area of work that's trying to be synergistic

Thanks so much, Sabina, for reminding us about this strong connection between some of these planetary crises and then also the poverty crisis.

And I think more so than ever, we need to recognize that these things are inseparable. The economics and the environment are absolutely inseparable. Thank you, Sabina. inseparable, and also for reminding us the importance of sort of the meaningful participation of different stakeholders that typically might not have so much power. My colleague, Mickey Fukuda, who's been working with us on arranging some of this, is very much a strong advocate of meaningful participation. I think bringing some of those ideas to the fore is really an important way to think about how we can activate and motivate action on synergies. So, colleagues, we have a few minutes left here, and now I'd like to actually have this event closed off by one of the key people who has helped raise the profile of synergies on a global level, and by one of the key people that's been behind the Global Initiative on Climate and SDG Synergies. So for our closing remarks, I'd like to turn the microphone over to Bahareh Sayedi, and she is the Senior Sustainable Energy and Climate Advisor at UNDESA. So, Bahareh, it's nice to see you again, and closing remarks.
Thank you, over to you.

Thank you so much, Eric. Let me start by thanking the Ministry of Environment of Japan for convening us and bringing us here together, as well as the organizers for this event, UNEP, ADB, and of course IGES. I also want to share that we were honored to collaborate with all of you at the 7th Global Conference on Climate and SDG Synergies, which actually took place place just before the HLPF. We gathered in ESCAP's beautiful headquarters at the end of June, and we were able to discuss this topic in detail. So I wanted to sort of focus my intervention here on 4 key messages that came out of the conference. The first one is that we have reached a point in time where the interconnected between the world's most critical challenges, whether it's climate change or addressing pollution or biodiversity or income inequality or poverty reduction, is no longer a debate. It is now widely recognized that the only way to address today's most critical challenges is to move away from siloed approaches to integrated solutions and synergistic action. Now, you have all participated in the HLPF. You know the state of the world. Last week, the Global Sustainable Development Report was launched, and let me highlight some of the statistics. Of the 139 SDG targets with trend data, just over a third, 36%, are on track or moving moderately. Nearly half of them, 49%, accessible SDG targets are moving too slowly, and 15% can slip— have slipped beyond the 2015 baseline. 1 in 10 people still lives in extreme poverty. Food security, affecting 2.3 billion people, remains well above 2015 limits. So this is— we see a regression on that in particular. On climate, of course, many of you are familiar with this statistics, global temperatures reached 1.43 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels in 2025, and greenhouse gas emissions have hit records high. Meanwhile, the official development assistance fell by a record 23% in 2025, weakening the financial foundations the world's poorest countries depend on. So what does this tell you? We can no longer afford addressing each of these critical challenges in isolation from one another. The only way to course correct is to look at it from the synergistic lens and integrated solutions. Now, the second point: we have a body of— an increasing body of evidence, data, and examples from rational regional and global actions. We heard many of them here today. The Regional Synergy Report is a perfect example of that. 140 countries around the world have shown how synergies can happen on the ground. And we know if we move in synergy, then we will have more efficient, more effective, and more impactful results. Now, we have heard different analogies for that. State Minister had mentioned one stone hitting— I would add harmful burns at a time. Colleagues here from Oxfam mentioned one bowling ball hitting multiple pins. That's the idea. We do work more effectively to address multiple challenges simultaneously and with more impact. But we know the progress is not at the speed and the scale that is needed. And that brings me to the third point. Despite our expanded understanding, despite the increasing body of knowledge and the evidence and the examples that we see from around the world, we continue to rely on fragmented systems. Fragmentation in policy, fragmentation in finance, fragmentation in data and monitoring systems, and even fragmentation in intergovernmental fora. I can use an example from my own day-to-day work. When we attend meetings during the HLPF, in many cases, when I say— when we talk about NDCs and NBSAPs, you would be surprised how many colleagues don't know what NBSAPs are. Similarly, when we attend the COPs and the, let's say, UNFCCC SPs, when we talk about the VNRs and how many people are familiar with the VNRs, not a lot of people raise their hands. So these intergovernmental fora and processes continue to work with communities that are very much focused on them in isolation from one another. And we need to change that, and that takes all hands on deck. Which brings me to the last point, and that is the critical importance of the next several years. We are in 2026, less than 4 years to go to 2030. Of course, these years will be important in terms of closing the acceleration gap for the SDGs and climate change and other issues, and this topic of synergies is going to play a key role. However, we also know that this discussions about what would be the future global agenda will kick off next year. And what we are talking about today is critical in laying the foundations for what is to come beyond 2030. So in that regard, and our colleague Scott mentioned, we all have a role to play. We all have children. Let's do it for our children. We all need to whether it's within our institutions, whether it's governmental institutions or private sector or civil society or youth or the MDGs, we can all do more to get us to where we need to be. Now, at DESA, of course, we remain fully committed to push this agenda forward in collaboration with the Ministry of Environment of Japan and IGF and UNEP and ESCAP, of course. Thank you. Course, we will continue to convene global dialogues. These are the annual synergy conferences. Stay tuned for the announcement of where the next one will be. We will continue to deepen the evidence base on climate and SDG synergies. In fact, at the conference in Bangkok, the Asia-Pacific report gained so much traction that there was a recommendation to replicate the same kind of report and case studies in other regions, Africa and elsewhere, and we hope to contribute to that as well. And lastly, of course, we will continue to leverage intergovernmental processes, including the discussions that will kick off in the, um, SDG Summit in 2027 that will formally start the discussions for what is to come beyond 2030. Thank you so much, and back to you.

Okay, thank you so much, Bahareh. I think this is a really good way to bring us to a close by highlighting not only the need for synergies to accelerate progress up to 2030, but for synergies to play a role beyond then, and especially to do this for our children. Thank you very much, colleagues. We appreciate all of your time, energy, and inputs. And we look forward to seeing you in the hallways and talk a little bit more about the issues covered here. Thank you. Bye-bye. Thank you.
